# Impact of premorbid nutritional status on TB severity

**Authors:** Alexa Tabackman; Akshay N. Gupte; Balamugesh Thangakunam; Senbagavalli Prakash Babu; Xinyi Du; Mandar Paradkar; Shri Vijay Bala Yogendra Shivakumar; Sanjay Gaikwad; Komala Ezhumalai; Chinnaiyan Ponnuraja; Samyra Cox; Nikhil Gupte; Jeffrey A. Viswanathan Diabetes Research Centre, Chennai, India | 12.Center for Emerging Pathogens, Department of Medicine, New Jersey Medical School, Rutgers Biomedical and Health Sciences, Newark, NJ, United States | 13.Department of Biostatistics, Boston University School of Public Health, Boston, MA | 14.Section of Infectious Diseases, Boston University Chobanian and Avedisian School of Medicine, Boston, MA

## Abstract

Undernutrition is the leading risk factor for TB worldwide and is associated with increased risk of unfavorable outcomes and mortality. In this study, we assessed the impact of undernutrition prior to TB onset on radiographic and microbiological markers of TB severity.

The RePORT India Consortium enrolled individuals with confirmed pulmonary TB (2015-2019). We used this data to conduct a prospective cohort analysis. Primary exposure was moderate-severe undernutrition (BMI<17 kg/m2) prior to TB disease calculated using anthropometric data and patient-reported weight loss. Outcomes included lung cavitation, high-grade sputum smear positivity (>2+), percentage of lung affected, and time to positivity in mycobacterial growth indicator tube testing. We used multivariable regression models and a generalized additive model to assess non-linear relationships between premorbid undernutrition and outcomes.

Of 1587 participants, 226 (14.2%) were undernourished before TB onset. Premorbid undernutrition was associated with increased odds of cavitation (aOR 1.80, 95% CI: 1.14-2.89) and greater lung involvement (4.57%, 95% CI: 0.73-8.42). The GAM analysis revealed a non-linear relationship between premorbid BMI and cavitation but not for other severity metrics.

Premorbid undernutrition significantly increases the risk of severe pulmonary disease in TB patients. This underscores the importance of nutritional interventions to mitigate TB severity and improve outcomes.

## INTRODUCTION:

In 2022, an estimated 2.8 million Indians developed tuberculosis (TB) disease, an incidence of 199 per 100,000 individuals. Over 30% of incident TB in India is attributable to undernutrition.1-4. Undernutrition blunts the adaptive and innate immune response to TB and is a key determinant and comorbidity of TB5-7. In addition to increasing the risk of acquiring TB, undernutrition has been associated with worse TB treatment outcomes8,9. A large prospective cohort analysis demonstrated that severe undernutrition prior to and at treatment initiation is associated with a two-fold increased risk of failure, death, and recurrence.5

Previously, a small retrospective cohort analysis of persons with TB (PWTB) in India found that undernutrition (defined as BMI<18.5kg/m2) at treatment initiation was associated with increased odds of cavitation and a greater percentage of lung affected on initial chest radiography10. Similar observations have been made in other contexts as well, and a higher sputum bacillary burden at diagnosis has also been reported among undernourished persons11-14. However, these observational studies were limited by the use of BMI at treatment initiation to define undernutrition. Weight loss is a common symptom of TB disease and individuals may be symptomatic for prolonged periods prior to initiating TB treatment15. As such, the relationship between undernutrition and TB is bi-directional, with individuals with a longer duration of or more severe disease more likely to be undernourished5. Therefore, the direction of causality between undernutrition and disease severity is challenging to understand, particularly when using cross-sectional measurements.

We designed a prospective cohort analysis to investigate the relationship between undernutrition prior to TB disease and markers of disease severity, which are associated with worse treatment outcomes and chronic pulmonary complications16-20.

## METHODS:

### Study design and setting

We conducted a prospective cohort analysis using data from 5 sites of the RePORT India Consortium between 2015 and 20195,21. These sites included Byramjee Jeejeebhoy Government Medical College (Pune), Christian Medical College (Vellore), Jawaharlal Institute of Postgraduate Medical Education and Research (Puducherry), National Institute of Research in Tuberculosis, and Prof. M. Viswanathan Diabetes Research Centre (Chennai). We obtained ethical approval at all sites in India and the partnering sites in the USA. All participants were consented and agreed to participate.

### Participants

We enrolled adults (≥18 years) within 1 week of initiating anti-TB therapy who were diagnosed with culture-positive pulmonary TB. We excluded individuals with Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolates found resistant to rifampin or isoniazid by either molecular or phenotypic testing or who reported close contact with persons with drug-resistant TB. We also excluded participants who did not have documented HIV testing within 3 months of enrollment. Lastly, we excluded persons with a poor functional status, defined as Karnofsky score <1022.

At enrollment, we collected extensive demographic, socioeconomic clinical, and behavioral data. We recorded duration of TB symptoms, patient-reported weight loss since symptom onset, and conducted anthropometry. We collected sputum for smear, Xpert MTB/RIF, and liquid culture using mycobacterial growth indicator tube testing (MGIT), and phenotypic susceptibility testing in MGIT. We screened for history of tobacco use and administered the Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test Concise (AUDIT-C) questionnaire23. Additionally, we asked participants about their history of diabetes mellitus and measured either random blood glucose or hemoglobin A1c. Participants also underwent a baseline chest radiograph (CXR) and were offered HIV testing.

### Exposures, outcomes, and covariates

Our primary exposure was pre-morbid BMI, which we defined as BMI prior to onset of TB symptoms. We calculated premorbid weight by subtracting reported weight loss due to TB from weight reported by participants at treatment initiation. We defined undernutrition as BMI<17kg/m2 which correlates to moderate-severe malnutrition based on WHO cutoffs24. We selected this cut-off based on increased unfavorable outcomes seen in this group in a previous analysis of RePORT India data5.

Outcomes included the following markers of TB severity analyzed independently - lung cavitation, high-grade sputum smear positivity (defined as smear grade ≥2+), percentage of lung affected (radiologically), and time to positivity (TTP) of MGIT in weeks. Each CXR was scored independently by two trained readers using a standardized form. The form rated the quality of 3 (anterior-post, lateral, and posteroanterior) views as acceptable; poor, but readable and not acceptable/readable. Abnormal CXRs were evaluated for the presence or absence of cavitation and opacity in the upper, mid and lower zones independently. In addition, the presence of mediastinal adenopathy, pleural effusion, hilar adenopathy, bronchiectasis and collapsed lung were also documented. Based on these findings, the readers computed an overall percentage of lung affected25. Cavitation was not included in the measure of the percentage of lung affected but was considered an independent measure of severity.

Participants were tested for HIV at the time of enrollment. We defined diabetes as blood sugar >200mg/dL, HbA1c ≥6.5%, or self-reported history of diabetes. Symptom duration was the longest period a participant reported experiencing any of the symptoms of TB (in months). Smoking was dichotomized into ever-smokers (past, former and current smokers) and never-smokers. Alcohol misuse was defined based on AUDIT-C scores ≥3 for females and ≥4 for males. Monthly income was categorized into four levels (<3000 Rupees [₹], ₹3000-5000, ₹5001-10000, and >₹10000).

### Statistical analysis

We generated descriptive statistics for the outcome variables as well as the potential confounders among those with and without premorbid undernutrition using t-test, Wilcoxon-rank sum test and chi-square test, as appropriate. We fit bivariate and multivariate models using logistic regression for categorical outcome variables (cavitation and high-grade sputum smear positivity), linear regression for % lung affected, and negative binomial regression for time to liquid culture positivity. The primary independent variable in all models was an indicator of undernutrition, measured by BMI<17kg/m2 . We built multivariable models for each outcome which also included age, sex, and symptom duration a priori as well as variables with p-values <0.2 in the descriptive statistics table or in the bivariate analyses. We calculated variable inflation factors (VIFs) to assess for multicollinearity among the independent variables. Redundant variables identified with VIF values >5 were subsequently removed to improve the stability and interpretability of the multivariable model.

We hypothesized effect modification by sex, history of alcohol misuse, and diabetes status on the impact of undernutrition on disease severity. Hormonal variations between males and females and differences in nutrient requirements, alongside behavioral factors like health-seeking behavior and dietary habits, may influence how undernutrition impacts disease outcomes differently in men and women26. Alcohol use can exacerbate nutrient malabsorption, suppress immune function, and delay care-seeking, all of which can modify the relationship between undernutrition and disease severity27. In a previous study, undernourished individuals with diabetes were found to have better treatment outcomes than those without28. Therefore, we conducted stratified analyses to explore these potential effect modifications by sex, alcohol use, and diabetes status.

Finally, a generalized additive model (GAM) was additionally fitted for each outcome, with continuous premorbid BMI as the primary independent variable. This model uses smoothing term based on cubic splines to assess for a non-linear relationships between premorbid BMI and the outcome variables.

## RESULTS:

Table 1 displays the baseline characteristics of the study participants. We included 1587 participants for whom premorbid weight loss data were collected, permitting calculation of premorbid BMI from a total of 2931 participants. Of the included participants, 1143 (72.0%) were male, 226 (14.2%) were undernourished prior to disease onset, 628 (39.6%) were former or current smokers, 441 (27.8%) had diabetes, and 51 (3.2%) had HIV.

### Radiographic Findings

Cavitary lesions were observed in 90 participants (62.9%) with premorbid BMI <17kg/m2 compared to 428 (52.7%) of participants with premorbid BMI ≥ 17 kg/m2 (unadjusted OR 1.52, 95% CI 1.06-2.21). In multivariable analyses, participants with premorbid BMI < 17kg/m2 had increased odds of cavitation (aOR 1.80, 95% CI 1.14-2.89) compared to participants with BMI ≥ 17kg/m2 after controlling for age, sex, symptom duration, monthly household income, smoking status, alcohol misuse, HIV and diabetes (Table 2).

Participants with premorbid undernutrition had, on average, 32.0% of lung affected compared to 27.09% among well-nourished participants (Table 1). In multivariable models, premorbid BMI < 17kg/m2 was associated with a 4.6% increased relative percentage of lung affected (95% CI 0.73-8.42) compared to those with BMI ≥ 17kg/m2 (Table 2).

When stratifying by sex, undernutrition is estimated to have a greater effect on cavitation (aOR 2.20, 95% CI 1.05-4.72) and lung involvement (9.8%, 95% CI 3.45-16.24) among women. Individuals with alcohol misuse and premorbid BMI ≤ 17kg/m2 had a 3-fold increased risk in cavitation (aOR 3.79, 95% CI 1.31-12.82) (Table S2). There was not a significant change in odds of cavitation or percentage of lung affected in undernourished individuals with diabetes (Figure 1).

Generalized additive models of the relationship between premorbid BMI and cavitation demonstrated a significant difference between the GAM and logistic regression model indicative of a non-linear relationship between premorbid BMI and cavitation.(Supplementary Figure 1a).

### Mycobacterial Burden

In multivariable analyses, premorbid undernutrition was not a predictor of MGIT TTP or sputum smear positivity (Table 2). Stratified analyses did show evidence of effect modification of premorbid undernutrition on MGIT TTP based on alcohol use (0.61, 95% CI 0.43-0.89), but there was no evidence of effect modification based on sex or diabetes (Figure 1). Our generalized additive models of premorbid BMI and MGIT TTP or sputum smear positivity did not show a significant difference between the GAM and negative binomial and linear models, respectively (Supplementary figures 1c-1d).

## DISCUSSION:

To our knowledge this is the first study that has evaluated the impact of premorbid nutritional status on markers of TB disease severity. In our multicenter prospective cohort analysis we found that premorbid undernutrition was associated with a nearly twofold increased risk of lung cavitation and a 5% increase in lung area affected. In prior analyses of undernutrition and PWTB, a limitation has been the use of BMI at treatment initiation, which cannot distinguish between undernutrition prior to disease onset or secondary to the disease itself. Our analysis addresses this limitation by using premorbid BMI in the analysis of disease severity, minimizing confounding from the bidirectional relationship between TB disease severity and undernutrition and temporality, strengthening our ability to make causal inferences. Thus, our findings underscore the importance of undernutrition as a key comorbidity of TB5,9,29,30.

A previous analysis of the RePORT India cohort has shown that undernutrition prior to TB diagnosis and at baseline is associated with unfavorable treatment outcomes5. By showing that the severity of pulmonary disease may be worse in undernourished individuals, our analysis explains in part why undernourished individuals are at increased risk of worse TB treatment outcomes. The likely reason for increased cavitation and lung involvement in those who are undernourished before the disease is a delayed and blunted adaptive immune response. Certainly, undernutrition has numerous other possible ways of affecting treatment outcomes, including increased drug toxicity, decreased pharmacokinetic exposure, and impaired immune response31. Given that undernourished individuals have greater lung involvement, they may also be at higher risk of post-tuberculosis lung disease, which may limit functional recovery, quality of life, and economic productivity despite tuberculosis treatment32,33. This hypothesis is supported by our prior work that found an association between low BMI and post-TB lung disease after adjusting for potential confounders20.

Our subgroup analyses are notable for the increased risk of cavitary disease in women and cavitary disease and mycobacterial burden in participants with alcohol misuse. BMI is a crude nutritional index that does not provide information about specific nutritional deficits, particularly micronutrient deficiencies. From a nutritional perspective, both women and individuals with heavy alcohol use are at risk of micronutrient deficiencies. Notably, no woman enrolled in our study reported alcohol use. In particular, both groups are at risk of vitamin A deficiency, which has been linked to an increased risk of TB disease34. Numerous other pathophysiological and behavioral mechanisms may also explain increased cavitary disease among heavy alcohol users.

Our analysis is also the first to report that the risk of cavitation increases sharply when BMI decreases below 17kg/m2. The generalized additive model assumes that there is a linear relationship between BMI and TB cavitation. Our data suggests this relationship may not be linear and the likelihood of cavitation may increase exponentially at low BMI. While this finding may be an artifact due to low sample size at the extremes of the BMI distribution, we did not observe this trend in other severity metrics and whether moderate-severe undernutrition (BMI<17kg/m2 ) represents a distinct group with a higher risk of cavitation is unclear and warrants further investigation.

Our analysis has numerous strengths. Our use of premorbid BMI to assess the impact of nutrition on severity is novel and methodologically important as it minimizes the confounding effect of disease-related weight loss. Further, our findings are strengthend by the multicenter cohort design from 5 epidemiologically and geographically diverse sites in India that capture both urban and rural populations, making our findings more generalizable to India. Our findings would also be generalizable to high TB burden settings with low HIV prevalence. Additionally, the analysis benefited from a rich dataset that allowed us to control for key predictors of disease severity, including HIV status, diabetes, smoking status, alcohol use, age, sex, and symptom duration.

However, the analysis does have limitations. First, the premorbid BMI was calculated using patient-reported weight loss due to TB, which may be subject to recall bias. The duration of symptoms reported by participants may also be inaccurate as TB symptoms can be insidious for extended periods. Similarly, these findings may not be generalizable to either those with extrapulmonary tuberculosis or those infected with drug-resistant strains of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, who were excluded from this analysis.

The association between premorbid BMI and increased severity of radiographic findings of pulmonary TB speaks to the degree of undernutrition in this patient population. Poor nutrition increases the risk of developing TB as well as poor outcomes, as undernutrition at the start of therapy has been associated with an increased risk of relapse35. In those who survive the initial disease, severe TB lung disease can lead to complications such as obstructive airway disease leading to long-lasting symptoms significantly affecting quality of life32,33.

Addressing population-scale undernutrition could serve as a TB vaccine by reducing disease progression and by lessening the severity of disease in the population. Additional research is needed to understand whether nutritional support in high TB burden settings can serve as host-directed therapy to lessen the impact of undernutrition on disease severity, treatment outcomes, and post-TB sequelae.
